title: A rainbow can form a complete circle
body: A rainbow's curved shape belongs to a **circle centered opposite the Sun**. Sunlight bends as it enters water droplets, reflects inside them, and bends again as it leaves, separating the colors. From the ground, the landscape usually hides the lower part of that circle. From an aircraft, with sunlight and droplets in the right positions, a full circular rainbow can be visible.

slides.alt: Schematic front view of a circular rainbow with its lower portion faded below a line representing the ground view. The center is labeled opposite the Sun.
slides.caption: The familiar arc is part of a circle. This schematic shows why the lower portion is usually hidden from a ground observer.

slides.heading: The droplet's role
items: Sunlight bends as it enters a water droplet.
Some light reflects inside the droplet.
It bends again on leaving, sending colors in different directions.

slides.heading: A different view from above
slides.text: An aircraft can put water droplets below you as well as above you. With the Sun behind you and the right conditions ahead, the lower arc can become visible too.

slides.question: Why do we usually see only an arc of the rainbow’s circle from the ground?
options: Droplets only form high in the sky
The landscape hides the lower part
The Sun lights only the top half
Our eyes can’t see below the horizon
slides.explanation: A rainbow belongs to a circle centred opposite the Sun. From the ground the landscape hides the lower part; from an aircraft, with droplets below you, the full circle can show.

source.label: NOAA SciJinks: What Causes a Rainbow?
